cards.front: Reflection lets a running program examine or modify the runtime behaviour of code in the JVM. What is the main performance cost of reflective calls?
cards.extra: Reflective types are resolved dynamically, so the JIT cannot optimise them the way it does direct calls. Use reflection sparingly on hot code paths and prefer direct calls wherever possible.

cards.front: Why is reflection considered a security and maintainability concern?
cards.back: It breaks abstraction and can reach private members
cards.extra: Reflective code can perform operations illegal in non-reflective code, such as touching private fields and methods, causing unexpected side effects. Reflective code is therefore not portable across upgrades and modules may block it outright.

cards.front: For which three kinds of tool does reflection routinely supply functionality?
cards.extra: Extensibility: instantiate user-supplied classes from their fully-qualified names. IDEs and class browsers enumerate members. Debuggers inspect private members and test harnesses call discovered APIs to raise coverage.

cards.front: By what default rule should you choose reflective vs direct access?
cards.back: If an operation can be done without reflection, avoid reflection
cards.extra: do not use reflection indiscriminately. Only reach for it when direct code cannot express the operation, such as loading a class unknown at compile time.

cards.front: Which Class method finds one method by name and parameter types, including inherited ones, but only public ones?
cards.extra: Its getDeclaredMethod sibling looks only at the class itself but does return private methods. Use int.class for primitive parameters: Integer.class gives a NoSuchMethodException.

cards.front: Which Class method returns an array of all methods declared in the class only, private ones included?
cards.extra: getMethods() instead returns public methods including inherited ones. getDeclaredMethods() never walks up to Object, so toString() appears only if the class overrides it.

cards.front: What does Method.getReturnType() return for List.get(int) on a List<String>?
cards.extra: getGenericReturnType() instead returns a Type that still records the type variable, so you can see the element type is E. Generics live in the signature, not in the raw return type.

cards.front: Why does Class.getDeclaredMethod("add", String.class) fail on a List<String>?
cards.extra: Type parameters of a method are erased at compile time, so the compiled signature takes Object, not String. Look the method up with Object.class; invoke it with a String and you lose type safety.

cards.front: When invoking a method reflectively, what must the first argument of invoke() be for a static method?
cards.extra: invoke takes the target object followed by a vararg of arguments. A static method has no receiver, so you pass null for the target, and then one argument per parameter.

cards.front: Where does an exception thrown by the invoked method itself end up?
cards.extra: The reflection machinery does not let the target's exception propagate directly. Catch InvocationTargetException and call getTargetException() (or getCause()) to reach the real exception.

cards.front: What does calling setAccessible(true) on a private Method actually change?
cards.back: It suppresses access checks; the method stays private
cards.extra: Without it, invoking a non-visible method throws IllegalAccessException. With it you may invoke the method, but its modifiers are unchanged and module boundaries may still restrict the package.

cards.front: How do you obtain the names of a method's formal parameters via reflection?
cards.extra: Class files do not store parameter names by default, because that costs memory and can leak names like password. Without the flag, Parameter.getName() returns a synthetic name such as arg0.

cards.front: Which two methods give you the exceptions a method declares it can throw?
cards.extra: Both live on Method and return an array, empty when nothing is declared. The generic variant preserves type information for parameterised exception types.

cards.front: What does getModifiers() return on Class and on Member?
cards.back: An int where each bit encodes one modifier
cards.extra: Bit 0 set means public, bit 3 set means static, and so on. Decode it with the static helper methods of java.lang.reflect.Modifier rather than testing bits yourself.

cards.front: Which class decodes the modifier bit-mask into readable flags?
cards.extra: It offers one static test per modifier, such as Modifier.isFinal(m) and isStatic. It was written before sealed classes, so it has no sealed or non-sealed checks.

cards.front: Which interface do Field, Method and Constructor share to expose getModifiers()?
cards.extra: Class declares its own getModifiers(); the three member types inherit theirs from Member. Both return the same bit-mask.

cards.front: Since which release can you read modifiers as a set of AccessFlag values?
cards.extra: Class.accessFlags() and Member.accessFlags() return a Set<AccessFlag>. Correspondences with the int flags are not one-to-one: some access flags have no matching modifier.

cards.front: What modifier does the compiler add to every interface, and why does getModifiers() on Collection show it?
cards.extra: Interfaces are implicitly abstract, so the compiler records the bit even though you never wrote it. This is why reflective code reports Collection as abstract and not final.

cards.front: What is the difference between getSimpleName() and getCanonicalName()?
cards.back: Simple: the name as written, no package. Canonical: the fully qualified name
cards.extra: For java.lang.String these are String and java.lang.String. Canonical names are defined by the language spec, simple names by what the source code actually said.

cards.front: Why does getCanonicalName() return null?
cards.extra: Those classes have no name you could write in source, so no canonical form exists. Use getTypeName() or getName() if you just need an informative string for such a class.

cards.front: Lambda expressions belong to a class with no source name. What does getSimpleName() of that class print?
cards.back: The name of the enclosing class that declared the lambda
cards.extra: The lambda's class is generated by the compiler and has no simple name, so the JVM reports the containing class, e.g. Main. The value therefore varies with where you declare the lambda.

cards.front: Which method returns a synthetic, compiler-generated name for anonymous classes and lambdas?
cards.extra: getTypeName() comes from Type (Java SE 8) and is informative rather than normative. getName() also works, but differs for arrays.

cards.front: What does Class.getName() return for a two-dimensional array of String?
cards.extra: One [ per array dimension, then for a reference type an L, the type name, and a ;. This is also the exact string Class.forName accepts to get the class back.

cards.front: In Class.getName() encodings, which letter stands for long?
cards.extra: L is reserved for reference types in the Ljava.lang.String; form. The primitive letters are Z, B, S, I, J, C, F, D for boolean, byte, short, int, long, char, float and double.

cards.front: Which Class method tests whether a given class is a record class?
cards.extra: Added in Java SE 16 alongside the record type itself. It returns true only for classes declared with the record keyword, not for plain immutable classes.

cards.front: Which reflection class models a single element declared in a record header?
cards.extra: Get them with Class.getRecordComponents(), which returns an array. Each component exposes its name, type, generic type, accessor and declaring record.

cards.front: Which RecordComponent method returns the generated accessor method?
cards.extra: Returns the Method modelling e.g. x() for component x. Companions are getType() (Class), getGenericType() (Type) and getDeclaringRecord().

cards.front: Does RecordComponent have a method giving you the backing Field?
cards.extra: Record components are not fields in the reflection model. To read the value you must go through the fields, which bring the record's own restriction with them.

cards.front: Can you set a record's field after calling Field.setAccessible(true)?
cards.extra: This is specific to records: their fields are final and reflexively locked. You can still read them, e.g. with getInt(obj), once the private field is made accessible.

cards.front: What is the core idea of an interceptor as described for service methods?
cards.back: A method call is replaced by another method that decides whether to proceed
cards.extra: The interceptor also sees the arguments before and the result after, so it can validate arguments, enforce security rules, skip the call, modify the result, or act on exceptions. Enterprise frameworks implement this with proxies.

cards.front: An annotation taking a Class attribute points at an interceptor implementation. Why must that value be cast when read?
cards.extra: If value() is declared to return Class<? extends Interceptor> you still get a raw Class from the annotation, so the cast is unchecked and the compiler warns about it.

cards.front: To reflectively call service.message("hi"), which three things does the interceptor tell invoke?
cards.extra: Those are exactly the pieces Method.invoke needs. Because the Method travels as a parameter, the same interceptor class can intercept any service method without knowing it at compile time.

cards.front: A ServiceFactory looks up message(String) but the service declares message(CharSequence). What happens?
cards.back: The lookup fails - no match is found
cards.extra: getDeclaredMethod needs an exact parameter-type match and derives the type from the argument you passed. String does not match CharSequence, so the MyService lookup misses even though String is a subtype.

cards.front: If no interceptor annotation is found on the service method, what should the factory do?
cards.back: Call the service method directly, with no interception
cards.extra: Interception is opt-in per method. Skipping the interceptor for unannotated methods lets the same factory handle plain services and intercepted ones without the caller knowing the difference.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: What is an exception?
cards.back: An event during execution that disrupts the normal flow
cards.extra: The short form of 'exceptional event'. When one occurs, the method creates an exception object describing the type and program state, and hands it to the runtime; that act is called throwing.

cards.front: What is the call stack when searching for an exception handler?
cards.back: The ordered list of methods called to reach the failing one
cards.extra: The runtime walks it in reverse: it starts at the method where the error occurred and works back through the callers, looking for a handler whose type matches the thrown object.

cards.front: When is an exception handler considered appropriate?
cards.back: When the thrown type can be assigned to the handler's parameter type
cards.extra: Matching is by subtype, not exact class. A handler for IOException also catches FileNotFoundException, because the thrown object can legally be assigned to that argument.

cards.front: If no handler anywhere on the call stack matches, what happens?
cards.back: The thread terminates - and if it is main, the program ends
cards.extra: The runtime searches every frame exhaustively. Reaching the bottom without a match kills that thread, printing the uncaught exception and its stack trace, which is the familiar 'Exception in thread main' output.

cards.front: What are the two ways to honour the Catch or Specify requirement for a checked exception?
cards.back: A try that catches it, or a throws clause that specifies it
cards.extra: Code that does neither does not compile. throws declares the exception in the method signature; try/catch handles it locally. Only checked exceptions are subject to this requirement.

cards.front: Which exception category holds preventable conditions that a well-written app should anticipate and recover from?
cards.extra: Example: FileNotFoundException from new FileReader(name). The app should catch it and prompt the user for a corrected file name, which is exactly what the checked category exists for.

cards.front: What kind of exceptions are Error and its subclasses?
cards.extra: Example: IOError after a hardware or system malfunction. An app may catch one to inform the user, but printing a stack trace and exiting is equally defensible.

cards.front: What kind of exceptions are RuntimeException and its subclasses?
cards.extra: Example: NullPointerException when a logic error passes null to FileReader. Catching is legal, but removing the bug is the usual answer.

cards.front: GitHub-style summary: which exceptions are unchecked?
cards.extra: Everything else extending Throwable is checked and must be caught or declared. This single rule is the whole of the catch-or-specify boundary.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: Where does the throws clause go in a method declaration?
cards.back: After the parameter list, before the body brace
cards.extra: Form: void writeList() throws IOException, IndexOutOfBoundsException { ... }. The exceptions are a comma-separated list after the keyword throws.

cards.front: Is listing an unchecked exception like IndexOutOfBoundsException in throws mandatory?
cards.extra: Only checked exceptions must be declared. Naming an unchecked one is legal and can document intent, but omitting it does not break compilation.

cards.front: What single argument does a throw statement take?
cards.back: A throwable object, i.e. any Throwable subclass instance
cards.extra: Form: throw new EmptyStackException();. The keyword is throw for throwing at runtime; throws is the declaration.

cards.front: What are the two direct descendants of Throwable?
cards.extra: All throwable types sit somewhere under these two. Everything else, RuntimeException and IOException included, is an indirect descendant.

cards.front: Which exception class does the JVM throw on a dynamic linking or other hard VM failure?
cards.extra: Simple programs typically neither catch nor throw Error. They signal problems external to the application that it usually cannot anticipate or recover from.

cards.front: Which Throwable methods support chained exceptions?
cards.extra: getCause() returns the exception that caused this one; initCause() sets it, and can be called only once. The Throwable constructors taking a cause do the same at construction time.

cards.front: What is a stack trace?
cards.back: The execution history of the current thread at throw time
cards.extra: It lists the classes and methods that were on the call stack, so you can see the path that led to the exception. Retrieve it with getStackTrace() to log in your own format.

cards.front: For a method that throws no checked exceptions, does its declaration need a throws clause?
cards.back: No - only uncaught checked exceptions must be declared
cards.extra: For example, a pop() throwing EmptyStackException, which is a RuntimeException, compiles without one.

cards.front: Should you write your own exception class when your class throws more than one related exception?
cards.back: Yes - so callers can catch them with one handler
cards.extra: no existing type fits, users need to tell your exceptions from other vendors', you throw several related ones, or users may not have access to the third-party exception types.

cards.front: Which superclass should a package's custom exception extend, if none of the specific subclasses fit?
cards.extra: For a LinkedListException, both RuntimeException and more specific types are inappropriate, so the generic parent is Exception. By convention, names of Exception descendants end in the string Exception.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: Bottom line: when should an exception be checked?
cards.back: When a client can reasonably recover from it
cards.extra: Recoverable conditions (file not found, retryable I/O) belong in the checked family so the compiler forces callers to deal with them.

cards.front: When should an exception be unchecked?
cards.back: When the client can do nothing to recover
cards.extra: Null dereferences, divide-by-zero and bad indexes are programming bugs. Forcing every caller to handle them would clutter the API without helping.

cards.front: Why are exceptions part of a method's public API?
cards.back: Callers must know what can be thrown to decide how to handle it
cards.extra: That is why checked exceptions must be declared: a method's throws clause is as much a part of its contract as its parameters and return type.

cards.front: Why does the compiler not require runtime exceptions to be caught or declared?
cards.back: They can happen anywhere and declaring them everywhere would obscure code
cards.extra: A typical program would list NullPointerException, ArithmeticException and IndexOutOfBoundsException on nearly every method, adding noise with no information.

cards.front: When is it common practice to throw a RuntimeException deliberately?
cards.back: When a caller used the method incorrectly
cards.extra: E.g. rejecting an invalid null argument with NullPointerException or an unusable value with IllegalArgumentException. It marks a contract violation by the caller.

cards.front: What does exception handling separate error-handling code from?
cards.extra: The try block reads as the happy path and the catch blocks hold the exceptional path. Traditional error codes interleave detection and reporting with the main flow, producing spaghetti code.

cards.front: How do exceptions propagate up the call stack?
cards.back: A method ducks them and the runtime searches backward for a handler
cards.extra: Intermediate methods need no error-handling logic, but each that lets a checked exception through must still list it in its throws clause.

cards.front: Which handler type catches every I/O exception regardless of subtype?
cards.extra: FileNotFoundException, EOFException and the rest are subtypes of IOException, so one handler covers them. Query the caught object to learn the specific cause.

cards.front: Why is catch (Exception e) usually a bad default?
cards.back: It is too general and can hide unanticipated exceptions
cards.extra: It also catches programming errors you never intended to handle, and the handler must accommodate any possibility. Catching Exception is fine when you just print and exit.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling

cards.front: What must directly follow a try block's closing brace?
cards.extra: Order matters: handlers are tested top to bottom, so a supertype first makes every subtype handler unreachable.

cards.front: Catch order for IOException before FileNotFoundException - what does javac say?
cards.back: Compile error: the specific type is already caught
cards.extra: FileNotFoundException is a subtype of IOException, so the second handler can never run. Write the more specific type first.

cards.front: Which catch-block type must the handler's argument have?
cards.extra: Unrelated types do not compile. The handler is invoked when the runtime object can legally be assigned to that parameter type.

cards.front: What is the multi-catch syntax for two disjoint exception types?
cards.extra: Available since Java SE 7 and it saves duplicating the handler body. Apart from the types joined by the pipe, it is an ordinary catch clause.

cards.front: In a multi-catch block, what modifier does the catch parameter implicitly get?
cards.extra: You cannot reassign ex inside the block, because the variable stands for several possible exception objects. Assigning to it is a compile error.

cards.front: What constraint applies to the types listed in one multi-catch?
cards.back: They must be disjoint - none may extend another
cards.extra: Otherwise the error reads 'Types in multi-catch must be disjoint'. Keeping the types unrelated guarantees each alternative is reachable.

cards.front: When does the finally block run?
cards.back: Whenever the try block exits, normally or abruptly
cards.extra: So it runs after the try body finishes, after a matching catch runs, after a return, break or continue, and even after an uncaught exception propagates.

cards.front: When might finally not run at all?
cards.back: When the JVM exits during the try or catch
cards.extra: A call to System.exit stops the process before cleanup matters. Otherwise finally is guaranteed, which is why it is the place for releasing resources.

cards.front: Which exception propagates when both the try and its finally throw?
cards.back: The finally exception - the try one is discarded
cards.extra: Common when close() in finally fails. This is a strong argument for try-with-resources, which suppresses instead of discarding, so the original failure survives.

cards.front: Which two interfaces mark a class as usable in try-with-resources?
cards.extra: Closeable is the older java.io one; its close() throws IOException, while AutoCloseable.close() declares Exception. Every Closeable is thus AutoCloseable.

cards.front: What state must a variable already have to be reused as a try-with-resources resource?
cards.back: It must be final or effectively final and assigned before the try
cards.extra: Resources declared inside the parentheses are implicitly final; the compiler adds the modifier for you. Either way the variable must implement AutoCloseable.

cards.front: In try-with-resources, if both the body and close() throw, which exception is propagated?
cards.back: The one from the body - close exceptions are suppressed
cards.extra: Retrieve them via Throwable.getSuppressed(). This reverses plain try/finally, where the close exception wins and the body exception is lost.

cards.front: In what order are the resources of a try-with-resources statement closed?
cards.extra: ZipFile declared first and BufferedWriter second means BufferedWriter closes first. That mirrors nesting, so a resource is never closed while a resource depending on it is open.

cards.front: Does try-with-resources still allow catch and finally blocks?
cards.back: Yes, and they run after the resources are closed
cards.extra: So a failure in close() happens before your catch block sees the body's exception. The catch handles the primary exception, with close failures attached as suppressed.

cards.front: What character marks something as an annotation rather than a call or member access?
cards.extra: It appears directly before the annotation type, as in @Override. The compiler reads the name after it as an annotation type, which is why annotations and interfaces share a namespace.

cards.front: In @SuppressWarnings("unchecked"), the element name value is missing. Why is that legal?
cards.back: With a single element named value, the name can be omitted
cards.extra: Writing @SuppressWarnings(value = "unchecked") is equivalent. The shorthand is only for value; any other element name must always be written.

cards.front: When may an annotation be written without parentheses?
cards.extra: Hence @Override and @Deprecated appear bare. The moment an element exists you need @Name(...), even if you supply no value.

cards.front: How does an annotation type declaration begin?
cards.extra: It looks like an interface whose keyword is interface with a leading at sign. Its body holds element declarations that resemble methods and may have default values. @ reads as 'AT', i.e. annotation type.

cards.front: Where must you annotate an annotation type's own definition to get it into Javadoc?
cards.extra: By default annotations on program elements are omitted from generated documentation. Putting @Documented on the annotation type tells javadoc to publish them.

cards.front: Which three java.lang annotations are used by the language and compiler?
cards.extra: They are predefined in every JDK. @Override and @SuppressWarnings steer compiler checks, @Deprecated both warns and documents.

cards.front: What does @Override do when the marked method does not actually override anything?
cards.extra: Using it is optional but catching typos in the method name or signature. Without it, a misspelt override silently becomes a new method in the subclass.

cards.front: Which @Deprecated attribute, added in Java SE 9, marks that the element will be removed in future?
cards.extra: The companion compiler warning category is removal. When an element is deprecated you should also document it with the Javadoc tag @deprecated.

cards.front: Which four warning categories can @SuppressWarnings name?
cards.extra: The array form suppresses several at once: @SuppressWarnings({"unchecked", "deprecation"}). The unchecked warnings arise when mixing with pre-generics legacy code.

cards.front: What does @SafeVarargs assert about a method or constructor?
cards.back: Its varargs body is safe, so no unchecked varargs warning
cards.extra: Applied to a generic varargs method you promise not to store arbitrary types into the array. Java suppresses the heap-pollution warning it would otherwise report at the call site.

cards.front: Which Java SE release introduced @FunctionalInterface?
cards.extra: It marks a type declaration as intended to be a functional interface, meaning one abstract method. It is documentation plus a compiler check against accidental extra abstract methods.

cards.front: RetentionPolicy.SOURCE keeps an annotation where?
cards.back: Source level only - the compiler ignores it
cards.extra: The annotation is available while compiling but never recorded in the class file. @Override is typically SOURCE-retained, since only javac needs to see it.

cards.front: RetentionPolicy.CLASS keeps an annotation where?
cards.back: In the class file - the JVM ignores it
cards.extra: This is the default retention when @Retention is not specified. Bytecode tools can read the annotation, but reflection at runtime cannot see it.

cards.front: RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME keeps an annotation where?
cards.extra: Only RUNTIME-retained annotations are visible through reflection, which is why frameworks that inspect annotations at runtime (JPA, Jackson, JUnit) declare it.

cards.front: Which Java SE release made annotations applicable to type uses, not just declarations?
cards.extra: That is a type annotation: usable on new, on casts, on implements clauses and on throws. It lets a pluggable type checker see where a type is used, not only where a variable is declared.

cards.front: What are type annotations used for?
cards.back: Feed pluggable type checkers that run alongside javac
cards.extra: E.g. declare a variable @NonNull String s. A checker module plugged into the compiler then warns when null could flow in. The JDK ships no checker, only the ability to accept one.

cards.front: Which meta-annotation restricts the element kinds an annotation may be applied to?
cards.extra: Its value is one or more ElementType constants: TYPE, FIELD, METHOD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, LOCAL_VARIABLE, PACKAGE, MODULE, TYPE_PARAMETER, ANNOTATION_TYPE, TYPE_USE, RECORD_COMPONENT. The compiler rejects an annotation used in the wrong place.

cards.front: Which ElementType value allows an annotation wherever a type is used?
cards.extra: That covers new, casts, implements and throws clauses. TYPE instead means class, interface, enum, annotation or record declarations.

cards.front: What does @Inherited do when a subclass has no annotation of that type?
cards.extra: Inheritance of annotations is off by default, so without it getAnnotation returns null on the subclass. @Inherited applies only to class declarations, never to methods or fields.

cards.front: To make your annotation apply twice on one element, which meta-annotation declares it repeatable?
cards.extra: Its value names the container annotation the compiler generates to hold the repeats. Applying an annotation twice without it is a compile-time error.

cards.front: A repeatable annotation needs a container. What must the container declare?
cards.back: A value element whose type is an array of the repeatable type
cards.extra: E.g. Schedules holds Schedule[] value(). The compiler then wraps repeated @Schedule annotations into one @Schedules automatically.

cards.front: Which AnnotatedElement method returns all repeated annotations at once?
cards.extra: Added in Java SE 8; it scans the container annotation for you. The older getAnnotation(Class) still returns only one and unchanged, so legacy code keeps working.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What is the source file that declares a module and all its properties?
cards.extra: Placed in the project's source root, e.g. src/main/java, so tools pick it up. It compiles to module-info.class, the module descriptor, which goes at the JAR root.

cards.front: Which four directives make up the body of a typical module declaration?
cards.extra: requires lists dependencies by module name, exports names packages that form the public API, uses names service types consumed, provides ... with ... names service implementations offered.

cards.front: By default, which types in a module's packages can code outside the module use?
cards.extra: A module has a real boundary the compiler and JVM enforce. To expose a type you must export or open the package that contains it.

cards.front: What is the effect of exports versus opens on a package?
cards.extra: Exports make the package part of the public API. Opens leaves it invisible to the compiler but lets reflection reach private members. A package may be both.

cards.front: What does requires transitive express?
cards.back: A dependency that is part of the module's own API
cards.extra: Any module reading this module automatically reads the required one. Needed when a public signature exposes types from the dependency, as java.sql does with java.xml.

cards.front: What is a modular JAR?
cards.extra: Without the descriptor it is a plain JAR. On the module path a modular JAR becomes a module; on the class path it still merges into the unnamed module.

cards.front: What is the module path, and what does it do to plain JARs?
cards.back: A list of artifacts; plain JARs become automatic modules
cards.extra: It parallels the class path but makes every artifact on it a module, enabling incremental modularisation. javac and java both understand it.

cards.front: Does a JAR having a module descriptor decide whether it is treated as a module?
cards.back: No - the path it is placed on decides
cards.extra: All JARs on the class path form the single unnamed module; all JARs on the module path become modules. So the project owner, not the dependency's maintainer, decides what is an individual module.

cards.front: How does module resolution work?
cards.back: Start at the initial module, follow each requires, error if one is missing
cards.extra: Repeat until nothing new is found; observe it with --show-module-resolution. The result is the module graph, whose edges are readability relations.

cards.front: Which module is the base module, and must you requires it?
cards.back: java.base - it is required implicitly, no clause needed
cards.extra: It holds Class, ClassLoader, java.lang, java.util and the module system itself. Resolution bootstraps it first, before any other module.

cards.front: Which three conditions must hold for module A to use a type from module B?
cards.back: Type is public, package is exported, A reads B
cards.extra: That third condition is the new part compared with plain JARs. Reading normally comes from requires, but --add-reads can add it at launch.

cards.front: Which two reliable-configuration errors does the module system detect at launch?
cards.extra: There is no notion of version beyond a string, so two versions of one module are a duplicate and rejected. A package living in two modules is a split package, also rejected. Static dependency cycles are the third check.

cards.front: What is a static dependency cycle between modules?
cards.extra: Cycles are fine at runtime, e.g. Spring reflecting over code that uses Spring annotations, but the modules must not require each other to compile. The module system rejects static cycles.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: Which rule summarises which JDK namespaces are safe to use?
cards.extra: In sun.* only sun.misc and sun.reflect are exempt, exported by jdk.unsupported. In com.sun.* roughly 90% is internal and the exported remainder belongs to jdk.* modules.

cards.front: Which module exports sun.misc and sun.reflect, and why?
cards.back: jdk.unsupported - they are needed with no feasible replacement
cards.extra: Chiefly for sun.misc.Unsafe. These are the deliberate exceptions: the rest of sun.* is internal and inaccessible.

cards.front: What proportion of com.sun.* packages is internal?
cards.extra: The namespace is JDK-specific rather than standard. Roughly a tenth is exported by jdk.* modules and supported, evolving with compatibility in mind, so each usage warrants a look.

cards.front: What happens to non-exported internal types when a module is on the module path?
cards.extra: E.g. sun.util.BuddhistCalendar lives in java.base which does not export sun.util. Both the compile error and the reflective runtime exception point at strong encapsulation.

cards.front: Which JDK release changed --illegal-access default from permit to deny?
cards.extra: JDK 9 to 15 permitted deep reflective access from the class path by default. JDK 16 flipped the default, and JDK 17 removed the option entirely.

cards.front: From JDK 17 onwards, which options allow access to internal APIs?
cards.extra: Nothing else works: illegal-access is gone. Both act per module/package pair and must be supplied at launch, by whoever runs the application.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What is the syntax of --add-exports?
cards.extra: E.g. --add-exports java.base/sun.util=ALL-UNNAMED. The space can be an equals sign to suit build tools such as Maven.

cards.front: What is ALL-UNNAMED in --add-exports or --add-opens?
cards.extra: Use it while your project is not modularised. Once your code runs as a module you can name that module and expose internals to it alone.

cards.front: Which kinds of member does --add-exports expose in the target package?
cards.extra: Same visibility as a real exports: the compiler can resolve the package and code can call public API in it. Non-public types remain out of reach.

cards.front: Which kinds of member does --add-opens expose?
cards.back: All types and members, public or not, via reflection
cards.extra: It works like an opens directive applied at launch. Compilation gains nothing, so code must reach the classes reflectively, usually with setAccessible(true).

cards.front: Is --add-exports needed at compile time, at run time, or both?
cards.back: Both - repeat it on java after using it on javac
cards.extra: Compiling against an internal package only grants compile access. Launching on JDK 17+ without the flag fails again at runtime.

cards.front: What happens if you pass --add-opens to javac?
cards.back: A warning: it has no effect at compile time
cards.extra: It is a pure runtime concept bound to reflection, so javac does not reject the option. It merely reports that nothing will happen, which helps when one option string is fed to several tools.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What does --add-modules add to module resolution?
cards.extra: Resolution starts from root modules, so adding one brings it and its transitive requires into the graph even though the initial module never mentions it.

cards.front: Which three special values does --add-modules accept?
cards.extra: ALL-DEFAULT is the set picked for class-path launches, for container apps. ALL-SYSTEM adds every system module, used by test harnesses. ALL-MODULE-PATH adds every module found on the module path.

cards.front: What does --add-reads $MODULE=$TARGETS add?
cards.back: Readability edges from one module to a comma-separated list
cards.extra: The module can then use public types in the targets' exported packages without a requires clause. ALL-UNNAMED as target lets a module read the unnamed module.

cards.front: Which tool accepts --add-modules?
cards.extra: It is a resolution-time option, so each tool that resolves modules honours it. --add-reads, by contrast, is documented for the compiler and runtime.

cards.front: Give a realistic use for --add-modules.
cards.back: Pull in an optional dependency not otherwise required
cards.extra: If a module only sometimes needs java.sql it never enters the graph on its own. Listing it in --add-modules at launch adds it, usually alongside --add-reads for readability.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: Which modifier on requires gives implied readability?
cards.extra: Any module that reads the declaring module automatically reads the required one too. Written requires transitive java.xml;.

cards.front: When should you use requires transitive for module B?
cards.back: When public signatures of your API refer to B's packages
cards.extra: Otherwise every client would have to add its own requires B to compile against your API. That is a hidden dependency clients could easily miss.

cards.front: Which class exposes java.sql's dependency on java.xml through its API?
cards.extra: It maps the SQL XML type, so java.xml types appear in a public signature. Driver.getParentLogger() likewise returns a java.util.logging.Logger, hence the transitive requires on java.logging.

cards.front: Contrast: java.prefs vs java.sql on java.xml.
cards.extra: Both declare requires java.xml, but only java.sql needs it transitive, because its public API mentions java.xml types such as SQLXML.

cards.front: Should a module rely on implied readability of B if it uses B's types throughout its own code?
cards.extra: Implied readability is for types used only at the boundary to the module that grants it. Using them everywhere is a genuine dependency; declaring it documents the architecture and survives refactoring.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What are the two reasons exports is a poor fit for reflection frameworks?
cards.back: It publishes the package as API, and only public members become reachable
cards.extra: Frameworks touch non-public types, constructors, accessors and fields. And exporting a package that handles HTTP requests or database access wrongly advertises it as a stable contract.

cards.front: How does opens differ from exports at compile time?
cards.back: The package stays fully encapsulated - outside code cannot compile against it
cards.extra: No exports means no compile-time access at all. Reflection is the only way in, which is exactly the intent: express that this package exists for a reflection-based framework.

cards.front: How does opens differ from exports with respect to non-public members?
cards.extra: For non-public members reflection still needs setAccessible(true). The point of opens is that the module has authorised the deep access, so no exception is thrown.

cards.front: How do you open every package of a module at once?
cards.extra: An open module behaves as if each package had its own opens. There is no wildcard form, so this keyword is the equivalent of opens com.example.*.

cards.front: In an open module, what happens to an explicit opens directive?
cards.back: Compile error - all packages are already open
cards.extra: Writing opens p; is redundant by definition, so the compiler rejects it. exports directives are still allowed and still mean what they say.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: Which keyword qualifies exports or opens to specific modules?
cards.back: to followed by a comma-separated module list
cards.extra: E.g. exports com.example.internal to com.example.friend;. The named modules get full access; every other module sees strong encapsulation as if the directive had no effect.

cards.front: Which JDK module qualifies exports of com.sun.org.apache.xml.internal* to java.xml.crypto?
cards.extra: Six internal packages of the JAXP module are needed by XML cryptography, so they are exported to java.xml.crypto and nothing else. A textbook case of controlled sharing inside the JDK.

cards.front: Can a package appear in both exports p and exports p to M?
cards.extra: The plain exports already grants everyone access, which makes the qualified one pointless. The module system treats this contradiction as an implementation error.

cards.front: What does javac report when a qualified export names a module that cannot be found?
cards.extra: The target is mentioned but not required, so it may simply not be on the path at compile time. Failing the build would break builds for optional targets.

cards.front: Who must change when a new module needs access to a qualified-exported package?
cards.back: The exporting module - it must add the new target
cards.extra: That control is the feature's point: the owner decides who shares. It is also its cost, since every new friend forces an edit to the exporting module's declaration.

cards.front: Why is the use case for qualified opens much smaller than for qualified exports?
cards.back: Open targets are frameworks that won't start depending on you
cards.extra: A framework never develops a compile dependency on a package it reflects over, so unqualified opens risk little. Qualified opens add fragility when API and implementation split, such as JPA and Hibernate.

cards.front: Why can qualified opens force you to mention an implementation in your code?
cards.back: Reflection needs opening to the module that actually reflects
cards.extra: Until frameworks adopt Lookup/VarHandle forwarding, JPA plus Hibernate means opening entity packages to the Hibernate module, not the JPA module. That leaks an implementation detail into the declaration.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What does requires static demand at compile time?
cards.back: The module must be present, and is readable
cards.extra: Identical to a normal requires during compilation, so you can freely use its types in source. Absence is a compile error.

cards.front: What does requires static allow at run time?
cards.back: The module may be absent, with no error or warning
cards.extra: If it is present on the graph the requiring module reads it. If not, you simply must not reach its types, or you get a NoClassDefFoundError.

cards.front: During resolution, does the module system try to find a requires static target?
cards.back: No - it is ignored, never pulled into the graph
cards.extra: Even a matching module on the module path is not added just for the optional dependency. It enters only via another module's regular requires or via --add-modules.

cards.front: What error do you get when code touches an absent optional dependency at runtime?
cards.extra: The type check fails while loading. With a normal requires the launch would have failed early; opting out of that check means the failure can surface late instead.

cards.front: Which API tells you at runtime whether a module is present?
cards.extra: Map it to a boolean and branch before calling into the optional dependency. A library cannot check for you; the decision belongs to the code that knows whether the feature is in use.

cards.front: When can you skip the presence check for an optional dependency?
cards.back: When the only callers already need that dependency
cards.extra: A JDBC helper inside a library is reached only from code that already uses java.sql, so java.sql is guaranteed in the graph. No check is needed there.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: Which class acts as the central service registry in Java?
cards.extra: It implements the service locator pattern. Call ServiceLoader.load(Service.class) to get a ServiceLoader that yields every provided implementation.

cards.front: Which two directives express the consumer and provider side of a service?
cards.extra: The consumer names the service type it will look up; the provider names which of its classes is the implementation. Services let a module call behaviour from a module it does not depend on.

cards.front: What may a provides ... with class be besides an implementor with a no-arg constructor?
cards.back: A type with a public static no-arg provider() method
cards.extra: That is the provider method form. Otherwise the provider is a concrete class extending or implementing the service with a public parameterless constructor.

cards.front: Which JDK module uses java.sql.Driver as a service of its own?
cards.extra: A module may use one of its own types as a service. It means JDBC drivers can be supplied by other modules without java.sql depending on any vendor.

cards.front: After switching to services, why can the implementation module stop exporting its package?
cards.extra: The loader instantiates providers through the descriptor, not through public API. Dropping the export shrinks the module's API surface, a bonus of the pattern.

cards.front: What is service binding during resolution?
cards.back: Resolving every module that provides a service some resolved module uses
cards.extra: It explains why simple apps resolve so many platform modules: providers are added so they are available at runtime. It is a second edge type in the module graph besides requires.

cards.front: Which JDK service lets logging frameworks receive the JDK's messages?
cards.extra: The JDK asks a LoggerFinder for Logger instances instead of writing to stdout, so a framework such as Logback can provide an implementation. Same mechanism as the JDBC Driver service.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What does the unnamed module contain?
cards.back: All classes loaded from the class path
cards.extra: Every JAR on the class path, modular or not, ends up bundled into one unnamed module. It exists so the module system can apply its rules uniformly without forcing anyone to modularise.

cards.front: What is the unnamed module's name?
cards.extra: No name means it cannot appear in a requires clause, so no explicit module can depend on class-path code. That refusal is precisely the design goal, not an oversight.

cards.front: Which other modules does the unnamed module read?
cards.back: Every module that makes it into the graph
cards.extra: It exports all its packages and opens them for reflection too. Both are the loosest settings in the module system, which is what keeps legacy class-path code working.

cards.front: A library ships a modular JAR. Does that force its users to run it as a module?
cards.back: No - a modular JAR on the class path joins the unnamed module
cards.extra: Whether a JAR is modular does not decide how it is treated; its location does. This is what lets the ecosystem modularise independently of each other.

cards.front: Code in an unnamed module prints getModule().getName(). What is the output?
cards.extra: From the module path the same call prints the module name. That contrast is the quickest way to confirm which path a JAR was launched from.

cards.front: If the initial module is the unnamed one, where does module resolution start?
cards.back: A predefined set of root modules from the runtime
cards.extra: Roughly, java.se if observable, else every java.* module exporting a package unqualified. Non-incubating runtime modules exporting unqualified packages are roots too; module-path modules never are unless --add-modules names them.

cards.front: Why does Java provide no requires class-path?
cards.back: Any class-path content would fulfil it, so it guarantees nothing
cards.extra: Reliable configuration demands that dependencies be checkable. A dependency satisfiable by any JAR is unverifiable, and two modules could disagree about where a shared library belongs.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::05 Modules and Linking

cards.front: What does jlink produce?
cards.back: A runtime image containing only the modules you picked
cards.extra: It links modules and their transitive dependencies into a JDK-like directory tree. Include your own modules and the image is a self-contained application deliverable.

cards.front: Does jlink compile bytecode to machine code?
cards.back: No - it only links, no ahead-of-time compilation
cards.extra: Your classes stay bytecode; the image just carries an OS-specific JVM plus the modules. That is why images are bound to one operating system.

cards.front: Which two options are mandatory to create an image?
cards.extra: The first names the initial modules, the second the target folder. jlink verifies that no module is missing or duplicated, then writes the image.

cards.front: How does jlink treat services by default?
cards.back: No service binding - providers must be listed
cards.extra: Deliberate, to keep images small. Add providers with --add-modules, or bind them all with --bind-services.

cards.front: Which option lists the modules that provide a given service?
cards.extra: Useful before building an image with jlink: it shows what is available in the runtime or on the module path. Then add the ones you need to --add-modules.

cards.front: Does jlink resolve optional (requires static) dependencies?
cards.extra: A static dependency would otherwise pull a module into the image only by accident. Explicitly adding it with --add-modules makes the choice deliberate.

cards.front: Can jlink link an application that depends on automatic modules?
cards.extra: An automatic module has no descriptor to link against. The app and its dependencies must be modular JARs, which is a real reason to push dependencies towards modular artefacts.

cards.front: What do you need so jlink can find your application modules?
cards.back: --module-path pointing at the folder holding them
cards.extra: Then --add-modules names the app's main module. Platform and application modules together are called the image's system modules.

cards.front: What does --launcher $NAME=$MODULE/$MAIN-CLASS generate?
cards.back: A script in the image's bin that starts that module
cards.extra: Shell script on Unix, batch file on Windows. The /$MAIN-CLASS part may be omitted if the descriptor already names a main class.

cards.front: What is the downside of launching through a jlink launcher?
cards.extra: The launcher passes them after --module, so you cannot add --add-modules ad hoc. Put options in JLINK_VM_OPTIONS or call java from the image directly.

cards.front: Does the module path on an image's launch override system modules?
cards.back: No - system modules shadow same-named module-path modules
cards.extra: A module-path entry with a system module's name is simply ignored. You can still supply extra modules, typically service providers, so users can extend the image.

cards.front: How do you generate an image for a different operating system?
cards.back: Put that OS's jmods folder on the module path
cards.extra: Run it with your own jlink; it sees foreign platform modules and links for that OS. Verify by checking for java.exe in bin, and keep JDK versions in step.

cards.front: Which two interfaces are the roots of the Collections Framework's two main categories?
cards.extra: Collections store objects for iteration. Maps bind each value to a key that represents it, like a primary key in a table. There is no inheritance relation between the two hierarchies.

cards.front: Which interface is the root of the iterator hierarchy in the Collections Framework?
cards.extra: An iterator walks over a collection. It is the fourth hierarchy, alongside Collection, Map and the Queue subcategory; Iterable sits above Collection but is not itself part of the framework.

cards.front: Why is Queue an odd member of the Collection hierarchy?
cards.back: Queues and stacks are not really about iteration
cards.extra: They exist for pushing and popping, not for walking the contents. They were nonetheless placed under Collection, so iteration happens to work on them as well.

cards.front: What should replace the legacy Vector class in non-concurrent code?
cards.extra: Vector was retrofitted to implement List. In a concurrent environment you would use a concurrent list instead, but for ordinary single-threaded code ArrayList is the substitute.

cards.front: What should replace the legacy Stack class in non-concurrent code?
cards.extra: Stack extends Vector and remains in the JDK only for backward compatibility. ArrayDeque provides the push/pop operations without Vector's synchronisation.

cards.front: Which legacy interface should no longer be used in place of Iterator?
cards.extra: Vector uses it to model its iterator. It predates the collections redesign and lacks remove() and the for-each protocol, so Iterator replaced it.

cards.front: What should replace Hashtable in non-concurrent code?
cards.extra: Hashtable was retrofitted to implement Map. In a concurrent setting ConcurrentHashMap is the replacement instead.

cards.front: Name two capabilities a collection has that a plain array does not.
cards.back: Tracks its size and can grow beyond a fixed capacity
cards.extra: An array's length is fixed once created; a collection tracks how many elements it holds and lets you keep adding. Collections can also reject nulls, test for presence, and intersect or merge with another collection.

cards.front: Which single fact most clearly separates a Collection from a Map?
cards.back: A map stores each value with a key; a collection stores bare elements
cards.extra: In a collection elements are the values themselves. In a map every value is bound to a key, so lookup happens by key rather than by position or presence.

cards.front: In which two releases was the Collections Framework substantially rewritten after Java SE 2?
cards.back: Java SE 5 (generics) and Java 8 (lambdas and default methods)
cards.extra: Generics made the containers type-safe; lambdas plus default methods made them functional, adding methods like forEach, removeIf and computeIfAbsent without breaking implementors.

cards.front: What must add(element) guarantee when it returns, even if it returns false?
cards.back: The element is in the collection; contains returns true
cards.extra: Returning false only signals a set-like collection already holding it. If the element would not be added at all, throw: UnsupportedOperationException, NullPointerException, ClassCastException or IllegalArgumentException.

cards.front: Which exception must a non-modifiable implementation throw from add?
cards.extra: The other cases: NullPointerException for an implementation rejecting nulls, ClassCastException for a wrong type, IllegalArgumentException for an element refused on its properties.

cards.front: Which Collection method models set union?
cards.extra: The four bulk operations map onto set algebra: containsAll inclusion, addAll union, removeAll complement, retainAll intersection.

cards.front: Which Collection method models set intersection?
cards.extra: It keeps only the elements also present in the argument and removes the rest. The argument need not be the same element type as this collection.

cards.front: Which Collection method models set complement?
cards.extra: It removes every element of this collection that is present in the argument. Note this is directional: it does not compute a symmetric difference.

cards.front: What does a true return from addAll(other) actually tell you?
cards.back: That at least one element was added, not all of them
cards.extra: The call reports whether this collection changed at all. Individual elements may still have been rejected, for instance duplicates in a Set, so success does not mean the other collection was fully absorbed.

cards.front: Can you call contains(new User()) on a Collection<String>?
cards.back: Yes - it compiles, and an IDE may warn
cards.extra: The check is legal even though it can never be true; the implementation may also throw ClassCastException. This looseness is deliberate, so algorithms can probe heterogeneous content.

cards.front: What does the no-arg toArray() return?
cards.extra: Casting it to String[] would compile but can fail at runtime. For a typed array use toArray(T[] a) or toArray(IntFunction<T[]>).

cards.front: In toArray(T[] a), what happens if the array is too small?
cards.back: A new array of the correct size is allocated and returned
cards.extra: If it is big enough, the elements are copied in and the same array is returned, with the first spare cell set to null. So new String[0] is safe and allocation-free when the collection is empty.

cards.front: Where is the unused tail of a large array passed to toArray(T[]) handled?
cards.back: The first unused cell is set to null
cards.extra: Cells after that are left untouched. The returned reference is the very array you supplied, so its tail may still hold your previous contents beyond the terminator.

cards.front: Which Collection method filters elements out in place using a predicate?
cards.extra: Added in Java SE 8. It replaces the older pattern of an explicit Iterator plus iterator.remove() inside an if statement, and is far easier to read.

cards.front: Which implementation should you pick by default when coding to the Collection interface?
cards.extra: The framework ships no direct implementation of Collection. ArrayList implements List, and since List extends Collection it is a usable Collection, and the sane default most of the time.

cards.front: Which interface sits above Collection and enables the for-each loop?
cards.extra: Added in Java SE 5 together with the for-each pattern. Any instance of Iterable can be used in a for-each, arrays included. It is not itself part of the Collections Framework.

cards.front: What does implementing Iterable require you to provide?
cards.extra: A single iterator() method returning one. That is why Iterable is described as a bridge to Iterator rather than a container in its own right.

cards.front: What does a List add over a plain Collection?
cards.back: Remembered insertion order, which also gives elements an index
cards.extra: Iteration always yields the first-added element first, and you can ask for element 3 directly. A plain Collection or a Set offers neither guarantee.

cards.front: Why should you not rely on the iteration order of an arbitrary Set?
cards.back: A stable order there is accidental, not guaranteed
cards.extra: Some implementations happen to iterate in a repeatable order, but the interface does not promise it. Only implementations that document a stable encounter order may be relied upon.

cards.front: Is a container with no duplicates and indexes available in the framework?
cards.back: No - SortedSet orders elements but gives them no index
cards.extra: The closest is a set with a guaranteed iteration order. Because it has no index, it does not implement List, so index access is unavailable.

cards.front: Which comparison mechanisms can a SortedSet use?
cards.back: Comparable.compareTo on the elements, or a supplied Comparator
cards.extra: If you supply a Comparator it wins even when the elements are Comparable, letting you sort differently from their natural order. Without one, elements must be Comparable or a ClassCastException arises.

cards.front: What is the difference between ordering and sorting?
cards.back: Ordering keeps insertion order; sorting orders by a comparison
cards.extra: A List is ordered: first element is the first added. A SortedSet is sorted: first element is the smallest under the comparison logic, and iteration runs lowest to greatest.

cards.front: Which SortedSet methods return the lowest and the greatest element?
cards.extra: SortedSet also adds headSet and tailSet for everything below or at-or-above a given element.

cards.front: What does NavigableSet add on top of SortedSet?
cards.extra: It changes no existing SortedSet behaviour. The additions include descendingSet(), descendingIterator(), and the ceiling/floor/higher/lower family of methods.

cards.front: Since which release do List.of() and Set.of() exist?
cards.extra: They are the convenience factory methods for collections. In Java SE 10 the family was joined by List.copyOf() and Set.copyOf().

cards.front: Can you add to or modify a list returned by List.of()?
cards.extra: Calling add, remove or set throws. If the contained objects themselves are mutable, however, you can still mutate them: only the structure is frozen.

cards.front: What happens if you pass a null to List.of() or Set.of()?
cards.extra: These implementations do not accept null elements, unlike some mutable collections such as ArrayList. Adding or copying a null is treated as a bug.

cards.front: What happens if you pass duplicate elements to Set.of()?
cards.back: An exception - duplicates are treated as a bug
cards.extra: A set cannot hold duplicates, so asking for one is a programming error rather than a silently ignored argument. The call fails at creation.

cards.front: Is the implementation returned by List.of() or Set.of() an ArrayList?
cards.extra: It may even differ with element count, and none is ArrayList or HashSet. Code must rely only on the List or Set contract, never on the concrete class.

cards.front: What are List.copyOf() and Set.copyOf() for?
cards.back: An unmodifiable copy of an existing collection
cards.extra: Added in Java SE 10. Later changes to the source collection do not show up in the copy, unlike a wrapper, which stays backed by the original.

cards.front: What does Set.copyOf() do with a source collection that holds duplicates?
cards.back: Keeps one of each - the result is a set
cards.extra: The other elements are dropped. A null source or a source containing null does not get this leniency: it throws NullPointerException.

cards.front: Does Arrays.asList() support add and remove?
cards.extra: The returned List wraps a fixed-size array, so its size cannot change, directly or through its iterator. It is therefore not unmodifiable: set and replacement still work.

cards.front: Which Collections methods find the minimum or maximum of a collection?
cards.extra: Both take the collection and an optional comparator. Without one the elements must be Comparable or a ClassCastException is thrown. An empty collection raises NoSuchElementException.

cards.front: Which two Collections methods locate a sublist inside a larger list?
cards.extra: Each returns the first or last index where the target list starts in the source, or -1 when the target does not occur.

cards.front: Which Collections method rotates a list's elements, and where does index 0 move?
cards.extra: Elements wrap around the end back to the front. Combining subList and rotate lets you move an element from one index to another position.

cards.front: A wrapper from Collections.unmodifiableList - can the underlying list still change?
cards.back: Yes, and the change shows through the wrapper
cards.extra: The wrapper does not copy: it delegates reads to the original and blocks writes at its own surface. To be safe, defensively copy the collection before wrapping.

cards.front: Which prefix names the Collections methods that wrap a collection in a synchronized view?
cards.extra: The unmodifiable family follows the same naming pattern. Two cautions apply: route every access through the wrapper, and synchronize manually on the list while iterating it.

cards.front: Are Collections.synchronizedXxx wrappers the recommended way to get concurrency?
cards.extra: The wrapper locks the whole structure and still leaves iteration unsafe. The concurrent collections give better throughput and give you consistent iteration semantics.

cards.front: Which two implementations of List does the framework provide?
cards.extra: If you are unsure which to pick, the advice is ArrayList. LinkedList's theoretical edge on insert and delete is largely erased by cache misses and pointer chasing on modern hardware.

cards.front: For which kind of use is LinkedList genuinely a good fit?
cards.back: A stack or queue - LIFO or FIFO access at the ends
cards.extra: A doubly linked list reaches its first and last node directly, faster than an ArrayList. If you use only those operations, LinkedList wins; ArrayDeque is another option, though it rejects nulls.

cards.front: Which List methods insert, read, replace and delete by index?
cards.extra: Each shifts the following elements as needed, except get and set. An invalid index throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.

cards.front: What does indexOf(e) return when the element is absent?
cards.extra: lastIndexOf(e) uses the same convention and returns the highest matching index. Neither throws.

cards.front: Which indexes does subList(start, end) actually cover?
cards.extra: So subList(1, 3) returns two elements. The result is a view: changes either way are reflected, which makes list.subList(a, b).clear() an idiom for removing a range.

cards.front: Does subList() return a copy of the elements?
cards.back: No - a view backed by the original list
cards.extra: Modifying the sublist modifies the main list and vice versa. That aliasing is what makes in-place range operations possible, and also what makes holding onto a sublist risky.

cards.front: Which method sorts a list in place, and since which release?
cards.extra: Before that you called Collections.sort(list, cmp). There is no no-arg overload: pass null or, preferably, Comparator.naturalOrder() to mean natural ordering.

cards.front: What does list.sort(null) assume about the elements?
cards.extra: If they do not, a ClassCastException is thrown. Writing Comparator.naturalOrder() expresses the same intent without a null argument.

cards.front: Which iterator type lets you walk a list backwards and insert elements?
cards.extra: Obtained via listIterator() or listIterator(index). It extends Iterator with hasPrevious, previous, nextIndex, previousIndex, add and set.

cards.front: What does ListIterator.set(e) throw if neither next nor previous was called?
cards.extra: set replaces the element most recently returned by a traversal step. With no such element there is nothing to replace, so it is a state error rather than an index error.

cards.front: How does LinkedList reach its first and last element so quickly?
cards.back: It holds direct references to both end nodes
cards.extra: Each node holds next, prev and item references, and the list holds first and last. Reaching the middle must follow next or prev links, which is where the cost appears.

cards.front: What does List.reversed() return?
cards.back: A view on the original list, in reverse order
cards.extra: Not a new list with copied elements, so changes are visible in both directions. The same view-versus-copy distinction applies to subList.

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::04 Collections::01 Array vs ArrayList

cards.front: Complexity of reading a middle element: ArrayList vs LinkedList?
cards.extra: ArrayList computes an offset; LinkedList must walk nodes. Reading first and last is O(1) for both, because LinkedList keeps references to both ends.

cards.front: Complexity of inserting at the first position: ArrayList vs LinkedList?
cards.extra: ArrayList shifts every element right; LinkedList relinks two references. In practice the linked-list advantage is diminished by cache misses on the way to the node.

cards.front: Complexity of inserting in the middle: ArrayList vs LinkedList?
cards.extra: ArrayList copies part of the array. LinkedList looks simple but must first find the node of the middle element, which is the O(n) part and usually dominates.

cards.front: What is the actual cost that spoils LinkedList on modern hardware?
cards.extra: Following a next/prev reference loads unrelated memory, often not in cache. ArrayList merely adds an offset to one base address, so locality makes it far faster in practice.

cards.front: By how much does a sparse (non-contiguous) linked list slow random reads?
cards.back: About 3x slower than a contiguous one
cards.extra: When nodes are scattered in the heap every step is a fresh cache miss. Real applications that keep adding and removing nodes are close to the scattered case.

cards.front: Iterating a LinkedList by index - what is the complexity?
cards.extra: Each get(i) restarts from an end and walks i nodes. On a 1,000-element list that is about half a millisecond versus roughly 4 microseconds with an iterator, so never use this pattern.

cards.front: Why does LinkedList still beat ArrayList when adding at the front?
cards.back: Insertion cost doesn't depend on size, at most one pointer hop
cards.extra: A direct reference to the first node means inserting at index 0 touches one node. ArrayList must copy the whole array one slot right, whose cost grows with n.

cards.front: By what factor does ArrayList grow its internal array when full?
cards.extra: Growth is geometric, so reallocations become rarer as the list grows. Each one allocates a new array and copies the old, which is why pre-sizing with new ArrayList<>(n) pays off.

cards.front: Does ArrayList shrink its internal array when you remove elements?
cards.extra: Removing can leave a large, mostly empty array. Call trimToSize() to copy it down, remembering that the next add may then have to grow again.

cards.front: How much memory does one LinkedList element cost?
cards.back: About 24 bytes per element (one Node object)
cards.extra: Each node holds next, prev and item plus a header. For 1,000 elements a LinkedList needs roughly 24 kB against roughly 5 kB for an ArrayList.

cards.front: When can a one-element ArrayList cost more memory than a one-element LinkedList?
cards.back: When it wraps a stale array of capacity 10
cards.extra: A default-constructed ArrayList with one element can take about 80 bytes against 56 for the LinkedList node. Fix it with trimToSize(), new ArrayList<>(2), or List.of() (26 bytes).

cards.front: Which list representation uses the least memory for a single element?
cards.extra: Cheaper than LinkedList (56) and a trimmed ArrayList (44). The trade-off is that it is unmodifiable, so it suits small fixed collections rather than growing ones.

cards.front: Which implementation should be your default for a regular list?
cards.extra: It wins almost every ordinary list operation including insert and delete, because the winning algorithm still has to reach the right element first. LinkedList only wins on stack/queue use at the ends.

cards.front: Which interfaces does LinkedList implement that justify it as a queue?
cards.extra: For a double-ended queue, prefer ArrayDeque over LinkedList. LinkedList remains reasonable when you also need List behaviour.

cards.front: Which class is the main Set implementation, and what does it wrap internally?
cards.extra: The elements are the map's keys and a shared placeholder object is the value. That is why HashSet behaves like HashMap with respect to hashing and equals.

cards.front: What does Set forbid that List allows?
cards.extra: Only one element equal to another may exist. As a consequence, add can fail and return false for an equal element already present.

cards.front: Which Set implementation guarantees a reproducible iteration order?
cards.extra: It combines a set with an internal linked list that records insertion order. Plain HashSet stores elements in no particular order you may rely on.

cards.front: Which class implements SortedSet in the framework?
cards.extra: It keeps elements sorted by natural ordering or a Comparator, and requires a way to compare elements at insertion time.

cards.front: A TreeSet has both a Comparable element type and a supplied Comparator. Which wins?
cards.extra: The comparator defines equality for the sorted structure too, so two elements it calls equal collide even if equals disagrees. This is a classic source of surprising duplicates.

cards.front: Which SortedSet method returns the elements strictly below a boundary?
cards.extra: tailSet(fromElement) is from-inclusive. When the boundary element exists, toElement is excluded and fromElement included, matching the usual half-open convention.

cards.front: Are the subsets returned by headSet, tailSet and subSet views or copies?
cards.extra: Changes flow in both directions. They remember their limits and reject additions outside them with IllegalArgumentException.

cards.front: Adding past a headSet's bound - which exception?
cards.extra: The subset refuses any element at or above toElement. The bound protects the view's own definition, so it cannot become inconsistent with the main set.

cards.front: Which NavigableSet methods return the nearest element including the argument?
cards.extra: Ceiling is the least element >= e, floor the greatest <= e. higher and lower are the strict variants. They return null when no such element exists.

cards.front: Which NavigableSet methods return and remove the extremes?
cards.extra: They combine a read with a removal, returning null on an empty set. They are the queue-like operations of the interface.

cards.front: What can the boolean argument of the NavigableSet subSet overload control?
cards.extra: So subSet(a, true, b, false) includes a and excludes b. headSet and tailSet gained the same inclusiveness flag.

cards.front: What does descendingSet() return?
cards.back: A view of the same set in reversed order
cards.extra: Not a copy: it is another NavigableSet sharing content, so removals propagate. descendingIterator() gives the same traversal without a new set object.

cards.front: Why is a mutable key an anti-pattern in a hash-based map?
cards.back: Mutating changes hashCode, so the entry becomes unreachable
cards.extra: The bucket chosen at insertion no longer matches the bucket computed at lookup, so even get(sameObject) misses. The key-value pair is effectively lost.

cards.front: A key is mutated to equal another existing key. What does get return?
cards.extra: Both keys now hash and compare equally, so the lookup lands on the other entry. Values are effectively overwritten or shadowed, and the unrelated key can no longer find its own value.

cards.front: Which type should you choose for map keys?
cards.back: Immutable types, such as String or Integer
cards.extra: If immutability is impossible, at minimum never mutate a key after insertion. Immutable keys keep hashCode and equality stable for the entry's whole life.

cards.front: What does HashSet.add actually delegate to?
cards.extra: The element becomes a key and a shared placeholder object is stored as the value. That is why mutating an element already in a HashSet breaks it exactly as mutating a map key would.

cards.front: You mutate an object after adding it to a HashSet. What can the set now contain?
cards.extra: Its hash no longer matches the stored bucket, so a re-add sees no duplicate and inserts again. Iteration then reveals the object at two positions.

cards.front: What is the most widely used Map implementation in the JDK?
cards.extra: It stores key-value pairs using hashing, detecting duplicates via a key's equals and hashCode. Both must be consistent for correctness.

cards.front: Which map implementation preserves insertion order?
cards.extra: It is a HashMap with an extra internal structure so iteration over keys or entries follows the order of insertion.

cards.front: How does IdentityHashMap compare its keys?
cards.extra: It is a specialised implementation for very precise cases, not general use. Two equal-but-distinct objects are different keys there.

cards.front: What is the practical limit on the number of key-value pairs for Map.of()?
cards.extra: The varargs form returns an Map.Entry-based map for more pairs: Map.ofEntries(entry(k, v), ...). Both are immutable and reject null keys or values.

cards.front: Which Map factory produces an immutable single entry?
cards.extra: Together with Map.of and Map.ofEntries it belongs to the Java SE 9 factory methods. Duplicate keys raise IllegalArgumentException at creation.

cards.front: Can a Map.of() map hold null keys or null values?
cards.extra: The factory maps and their entries are immutable and null-hostile. A duplicate key is treated as a bug and fails at creation with IllegalArgumentException.

cards.front: Which collection shape does the set of map keys have?
cards.extra: Every key binds exactly one value, so keys are a set. Key-value entries are also a set, while values may repeat and so form a plain Collection.

cards.front: Can two keys in one map bind the same value?
cards.back: Yes - a value may be bound to several keys
cards.extra: The rules are asymmetric: each key has at most one value, but many keys can point at one object. That is why values() is not a Set.

cards.front: Can you call setKey() on a Map.Entry?
cards.extra: Entries offer getKey, getValue and setValue. Changing a key in place would move the entry to another bucket and corrupt the map.

cards.front: Are Map.Entry objects from a map copies or views?
cards.extra: Calling setValue on an entry updates the map, and updating the map shows in the entry. That is why removing a key breaks the entry you hold.

cards.front: What is a multimap, and does the framework provide one?
cards.back: One key mapped to several values; not directly
cards.extra: The framework offers no Multimap type. The idiom is a map whose values are collections, e.g. Map<K, List<V>>, usually populated with computeIfAbsent.

cards.front: Which functional interface does Map.forEach take?
cards.extra: Each entry is delivered as two arguments rather than as a Map.Entry. That is the one difference from Iterable.forEach, which takes a plain Consumer.

cards.front: What does replace(key, value) do, and what does it return?
cards.extra: Semantically it is put-if-present: with no existing mapping nothing happens and null comes back. It never creates an entry.

cards.front: What does replace(key, oldValue, newValue) return?
cards.extra: It replaces only when the current value equals the given old value, a compare-and-set for maps. Otherwise nothing changes and false is returned.

cards.front: Which Map method transforms every value in one call?
cards.extra: The function receives key and old value and returns the new one. It iterates all entries internally; an exception aborts the traversal partway.

cards.front: What happens if a compute-family remapping function returns null?
cards.back: The key is removed from the map
cards.extra: No entry with a null value is created. This gives the compute methods a natural delete semantics: return null to drop the mapping.

cards.front: What do the compute methods return?
cards.back: The new value - unlike put, which returns the old one
cards.extra: If the function returned null there is no new value and null is returned instead. Mixing up the two return conventions is a common source of bugs.

cards.front: computeIfPresent vs compute: which one may call the function with a null value?
cards.extra: computeIfPresent runs only when a non-null value is already bound, so the function is skipped for an absent key. compute runs unconditionally, so it sees null there.

cards.front: When exactly does computeIfAbsent call its function?
cards.back: When the key is absent or maps to null
