cards.extra: The function is a plain Function taking only the key, since there is no current value. That is why it is the idiom for building map-of-collections structures.

cards.front: Why prefer computeIfAbsent(k, k -> new ArrayList<>()) over putIfAbsent?
cards.back: The list is created only when needed
cards.extra: With putIfAbsent you must build the empty list up front, even if the key exists, wasting an allocation every call. The compute form allocates only for new keys.

cards.front: Which Map method merges a value into an immutable aggregate such as a String?
cards.extra: computeIfAbsent cannot help here because a String cannot be appended to in place. merge supplies the new value and the function combines it with the existing one.

cards.front: In merge, when is the remapping function not called?
cards.back: When the key is absent or maps to null
cards.extra: The new value is simply bound and stored. Only when a non-null value already exists does the function receive old and new values.

cards.front: Why should the lambdas passed to computeIfAbsent and merge be non-capturing?
cards.back: For performance - a capturing lambda allocates per call
cards.extra: A lambda that captures a local must create a new object each time it is evaluated, while a non-capturing one is a cached singleton. Taking the key as a parameter avoids the capture entirely.

cards.front: Which data structure backs TreeMap?
cards.extra: It implements both SortedMap and NavigableMap and offers O(log n) lookups. ConcurrentSkipListMap is the thread-safe counterpart, built on a skip list.

cards.front: What must you provide to a TreeMap so it can sort keys?
cards.extra: A supplied comparator takes precedence even over comparable keys. Without either, insertion fails with ClassCastException.

cards.front: Which SortedMap methods return the lowest and greatest key?
cards.extra: Their entry-level siblings on NavigableMap are firstEntry() and lastEntry(), which return the whole key-value pair.

cards.front: What does headMap(toKey) contain?
cards.extra: SortedMap has no inclusive variant: tailMap(fromKey) starts at fromKey, but headMap excludes its bound. NavigableMap adds the inclusive boolean overloads.

cards.front: Are the maps from headMap, tailMap, subMap copies?
cards.extra: Changes propagate both ways. You may remove from a view, but inserting a key outside its bounds is rejected.

cards.front: ceilingKey vs higherKey: which includes the argument?
cards.extra: The same pair exists for floor/lower: floorKey may return the argument itself, lowerKey returns a strictly smaller key. Both return null when nothing qualifies.

cards.front: Which NavigableMap methods return and remove an entry?
cards.extra: They pull the lowest or highest entry out of the map, returning it. On an empty map they return null rather than throwing.

cards.front: Which NavigableMap method returns a descending-order view?
cards.extra: descendingKeySet() gives the key-only view. Both are backed by the map but allow removal only, not insertion.

cards.front: Can you cast the result of TreeMap.keySet() to NavigableSet?
cards.extra: navigableKeySet() does the cast for you and returns the same object. The cast is only safe because TreeMap's keys are navigable; on a HashMap it is not.

cards.front: What does put(k, v) return for a new key?
cards.extra: put returns the previous value bound to the key, so a null result means there was none. On an existing key it returns the value being replaced.

cards.front: Does putIfAbsent(k, v) replace an existing null value?
cards.back: Yes - it treats a null mapping as absent
cards.extra: That is what makes it useful for fixing faulty maps that acquired null values, unlike containsKey, which would report the key as present.

cards.front: Why does iterating map.values() into an int throw NPE on a null value?
cards.extra: The values are Integer objects, and assigning one to an int unboxes it. A null Integer cannot be unboxed, so the NPE comes from boxing rather than from the map.

cards.front: What does getOrDefault(k, def) return?
cards.back: def when the key is absent, else the mapped value
cards.extra: Added in Java SE 8. Note it does not change the map: no entry is created for the default.

cards.front: What does remove(k, v) return, and when does it remove?
cards.back: true if the pair matched and was removed
cards.extra: It removes only when the current value equals v, so a blind remove(k) that might clobber a fresh value is avoided. That overload returns the removed value instead.

cards.front: Which Map method reports whether a value occurs anywhere in the map?
cards.extra: It scans for a match and is not a key lookup, so on a hash map it is typically linear. containsKey(k) is the hashed, fast counterpart.

cards.front: What does putAll(other) do with colliding keys?
cards.back: The other map's values overwrite the existing ones
cards.extra: Merging is last-writer-wins per key rather than a union of values. Expect data loss if you were trying to accumulate.

cards.front: What does keySet() return?
cards.extra: entrySet() returns Set<Map.Entry> and values() a Collection. All three are views, so map changes appear in them immediately.

cards.front: What happens if you call add on the set from keySet()?
cards.extra: These views are fixed: you cannot add keys or values through them. Removal is supported and propagates to the map, because a key alone identifies an entry.

cards.front: You remove a key from keySet(). What happens to the map?
cards.back: The whole key-value pair is removed from the map
cards.extra: The set is a view, so its removals delete the corresponding entries. The same is true of removing an entry from entrySet().

cards.front: Which entry is removed if you drop a value from values(), and the value repeats?
cards.back: Only the first matching entry - order is unspecified
cards.extra: A value can occur under several keys, so removing cannot be unambiguous. On a HashMap you cannot predict which entry will be hit.

cards.front: Why iterate entrySet() rather than keySet() plus get?
cards.back: Entry iteration is one pass with no extra lookups
cards.extra: Getting each value from the key re-hashes and re-searches. Iterating entries delivers both halves of each pair in a single traversal.
